chunks.text: I think everyone's fine with that. And we're just going to start the hearing of evidence. We've got ECPAT New Zealand, Eleanor Parks. So Eleanor Parks, if you're on, we will hear from you for 10 minutes. Kia ora. Thank you. Can you hear me?

Welcome. We've got 10 minutes with you today. We'll probably have some questions, so if you could probably just leave a couple of minutes near the end, and if we're nearing maybe nine minutes or so, and you're still talking away there, I'll just give you an indication you've got a couple of minutes to go. But welcome. Thank you. Yeah, let me know how we go for time. I would like to allow time for questions if you have them.

I'm assuming everyone's read the written submission, so I'll try not to repeat too much of it. For people who haven't met me before, I'm Eleanor Parks from ECPAT New Zealand. We've obviously been watching very closely since late 2025, when Section 17 was suspended under urgency. Overseas adoptions are very much in our wheelhouse. We're an anti-trafficking organization, and so cases like Matamata and more recently the Tuai case have demonstrated how these informal pathways really can be weaponized for modern slavery. So we're very supportive of the fact that

the government is looking into address these loopholes and do something about them. For a bit of background, part of ECPAT International, so the largest network of organizations working to end child sexual exploitation and trafficking. That is the specific focus. And our work in New Zealand is very much grounded in research, advocacy, and lived experience of young people here and frontline workers like social workers here.

We've consistently focused on safeguarding children from exploitation and domestic trafficking and international trafficking. So that includes things like the misuse of adoption practices. What we do know is that while cases of child trafficking in New Zealand rarely make headlines, there are also the many, many stories of successful, life-changing cross-border support for children, stories where children have been provided with safety and family and opportunity, that don't make headlines.

And so our challenge and your challenge is to stop the abuse, the cases of abuse and exploitation, but without stopping those good, positive cases that are giving these children what they really need to be safe and to thrive. And at the moment, this bill, while very well intended, isn't quite hitting that mark.

So I'd like to go into a few details around some of our concerns. So we definitely are supporting strong protections. We want to prevent child trafficking, and we want to stop overseas adoption processes from being misused. And we want effective scrutiny where there are child protection concerns.

But at the moment, the framework in its current form would likely unintentionally deny certain children access to care, family support, education, health services, and stable living arrangements if they do not come from a country that has yet been designated under a future regulatory process.

So looking at Section 17 just as a trafficking loophole misreads a pathway that has also enabled legitimate Pacific kinship care based in cross-border family support, and these are the children that we're concerned will be missing out on that safety and security.

A few details on that. On the surface, the provisions definitely look to reduce the risk of adoption being used inappropriately for immigration or exploitation, but it doesn't make a distinction between adoptions that are undertaken to secure those immigration outcomes and facilitate abuse and adoption that is being used as the genuine kinship care arrangements that are in the best interests of the child.

In a Western view, adoption is seen as a solution for a child with no family or no suitable family, and Western adoption laws, including the Hague Convention, which has been a big part of this conversation, are built on that clean break idea. The child is removed from unsuitable parents and transplanted to better ones. But in the Pacific, adoption is often additive.

We're not replacing children's parents with better ones. It's about gaining additional caregivers. At the moment, the proposed amendments really impose that Western nuclear family model in places that don't necessarily fit, that don't align with Pacific ways of understanding family.

In the Pacific, these kinds of care, this kinship customary care, is recognized and it's a valued practice, with children moving between households and communities and countries within their family networks. And it's not about circumventing immigration rules. It's about welfare, it's about education, it's about support.

And this applies to a lot of children in New Zealand. It's estimated that 3.2% or as much as 5% of all children in New Zealand are living in kinship care arrangements outside of formal statutory care. Kinship care isn't a risk factor, it's a protective asset.
We want to be careful not to be removing the protective aspect.

What we need is to reconcile The best interests of the child as the primary consideration, and it's just not quite happening yet. So any legislative framework governing overseas adoptions, they do need to be measured against our obligations under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.

So that includes the best interests of the child, preservation of family relationships, which covers the importance of family relationships, identity, and appropriate alternative care. It says that legislation should avoid unnecessarily disrupting family-based care arrangements where safeguards can be demonstrated.

And it also covers protection from exploitation, of course. But those safeguards need to be targeted at identifying the risk where it actually exists, which is very often at the level of the individual caring arrangement in the receiving country. So not only focusing on where the children are coming from, but focusing on what are the child protection arrangements here in New Zealand when those children are here.

We can't just be monitoring what is happening in the sending countries if the abuse is happening here, which is what we've seen. Eleanor, we've got a couple of minutes still with you, but I have got a question from Dan Rosewarne. I'm wondering, do you want to take that question and then come back to a summary from you?

Yeah, absolutely. Let's do that. Dan, thank you. Yeah, thanks Chair, and thanks Eleanor for your submission. You've kind of traversed the culturally grounded kinship care arrangements such, like the Pacific community in particular. I was just wondering how you would like to see that reflected in the legislation. Are you thinking like a definition of exceptional circumstances, or a list of examples, or like a separate provision dealing specifically with kinship care arrangements?

Yeah. Great question, because it does say it refers to exceptional circumstances within the current wording, but it doesn't define what those might include. So we would suggest just to avoid that sort of arbitrary or inconsistent interpretation of that, this bill should explicitly recognize culturally grounded kinship care arrangements, such as those common in Pacific communities, as qualifying exceptional circumstance.

That would be our preference. That would be the strongest way to do it. If the committee is not of a mind to include it within this legislation and they would like to-- There are ways of doing it outside of this legislation as a separate pathway because, like we said, this isn't a classic Western-style adoption. It doesn't have to fit here.

But we would be very concerned if this piece of legislation was to be progressed and the committee just thought, "Well, someone else can deal with that later because it needs to sit elsewhere." That needs to be happening alongside, and really this process needs to be slowed down to allow for that if it is going to happen outside of this legislation.

Otherwise, we're concerned it just would not be the priority, and it would never happen. We would effectively have this in place for the longer term without those other additional factors. Thanks, Eleanor. That's helpful. We've got about just about a minute or so left, Eleanor, if you'd just like to just do a summary and go from there.

Yeah. I think really we've covered everything. We need to be able to distinguish within any legislation between harmful arrangements and protective ones, and a child-centered system should be capable of making that distinction. So it needs a bit more nuance in that way.

We're not going to find effective safeguards in black and white impermeable barriers. We need some carefully designed pathways that really do identify risk and monitor welfare and preserve children's rights to family and culture and identity and belonging, and with that comes safety and security and a chance for those children to thrive.

We don't need to deny those opportunities to keep them safe from exploitation if we can add some nuance and be a little more thorough in our approach to this. That's fantastic, Eleanor. Thank you very much for your submission today, and thank you again. Our next submitter today is Max Marshall.
I think you may be in person in the room or otherwise online, but we'll just wait for Max. He's online, Mr. Chair. Just bringing him in now. Fantastic.

Are you there, Max, or are we still waiting? I'm here. Hi. G'day, Max. Welcome to your submission today. We've got five minutes with you, so if you'd like to leave some time, I'll indicate when you've got about a minute to go. So, we're in your hands. Okay. Good stuff. Thanks.

Good morning, and thank you for giving me an opportunity to speak to you. I want to speak in support of many of the other submitters who have spoken today. History has shown that many of these overseas adoptions have had bad outcomes, and I want to protect the welfare of the child.

There have been situations in which we've created a problem for a child. As for any child, no one is born with a tabula rasa. The circumstances of one's background provides challenges particular to it. For the case of the adoptee, the circumstances of adoption start off with complications, and these have been well documented, as there is a need to protect the child's welfare in the process.

I want to talk about how this relationship is unique. What I mean by unique is that it is an option beyond more accessible options of local adoptions that we are choosing over. I do not subscribe to the notion of overseas adoption wholly subscribing to the needs of the parents.

I want to talk against the commodification of desire. A Soviet pilot who lands on American soil seeking asylum does not make him automatically an American citizen who has grown up all their life in that society. The same A is not going to be.

In our instant age, we demand our needs be met, be gratified instantly, and the children's needs are often lost in the frame of the parent's powerful desire for an ideal family. What is testimony to an ideal family is a powerful motivation lies inside is this desire to have a family.

Inside monarchs, the vision promoted by a particular monarch was to be seen with other powerful monarchs to project this vision of power to his subjects. King Richard the Lionheart and King Philip of France having a sleepover would be the equivalent version to the contemporary one, a jaunty spread in a Hello!

Magazine. It does not carry the same private or romantic meaning as it does today. And it is uncomfortable to reflect on its behavior then, but I am uncomfortable in the same way about overseas adoption, about how it does not configure to this deeper cultural idea about home and family.

I argue that inside these projects, the welfare of the child is hidden by the projects of that- Just over a minute now, Max. So you just- So this must stand as an anathema to what the concept of family means in terms of formation, love, and belonging. I'm not hostile to the project of overseas adoption, but I am aware that lawmakers must put in place safeguards which recognize the welfare of the child as its primary aim.

Thank you. Thank you very much, Max. I'm not seeing any questions. Is there any questions, members? No, I'm not seeing any. So thank you very much, Max, for your time today and for your submission. Thank you. Our next submitter is the New Zealand Law Society, so we'll just wait a moment for them to come online.

Welcome. Welcome, Margaret Casey KC. Nice to see you today. I think we may be also getting joined by another one of your colleagues, if that's right. Lena, yes. Yep. I'm not seeing her at the moment, but-- Oh, no, we have got her now. So welcome. We have got 10 minutes of your time today.

Please leave some time for some questions. If we're still going around about eight minutes, I'll just let you know, just so you know where your timing is. So welcome. Thank you. Kia ora koutou katoa. Good morning from Tāmaki Makaurau. And you have two of us here today to speak to the New Zealand Law Society submission that we filed. We are conscious that it is a lengthy submission, but there's a reason for that.

This is a very discreet area of law. There are very few lawyers in the country that actually work in the adoption area, and even less who work in the field of surrogacy and international surrogacy. So we've approached the bill very much as the people best to stress test it.

What is it going to work? How is it going to work in practice? For myself, I bring to the group over 20 years work in the area of adoption and surrogacy. I'm very involved in the international work about cross-border surrogacy arrangements, having spent 10 years working on a Hague project where they were trying to establish cross-border surrogacy.

I say that just to explain the reason why we have put in examples so that you know that these are real-world examples that we have used to highlight some of the issues that we have identified with the bill. Having said all of that, we're very comfortable with the bill as a way of trying to protect children from trafficking and exploitation.

Our concern has been, and you'll see that highlighted again and again in the submission, is that unintentionally this bill may expose another group of children to different risks, legal limbo, insecure or no parentage, unequal treatment, and in some case, statelessness.

And we believe that the bill can work for both groups of people, and we shouldn't be having to choose between the different cohorts of children. And that is the focus we have brought to our submissions. We wanted to address two or three particular points, and primarily they are focused at the Family Court jurisdiction and wanting to preserve that because we, in the field, believe the Family Court is doing a very good job at doing what it needs to do to protect children.

Remembering that some of these recognition cases don't actually come before the Family Court. They are not the issue that we see in terms of what we've identified. So Selina is going to just talk to you about some of the restrictions on the Family Court jurisdiction by reference to our submission.

Thank you. Tena koutou. Good morning. As Margaret has just said, I will be addressing the committee regarding the bill's limitations on the Family Court's jurisdiction. And the society's concerns around this limitation are twofold. The bill introduces barriers that firstly prevent the Family Court from recognizing genuine parent-child relationships, even where that's in the child's interest to do so. And secondly, it creates a barrier to the court carrying out its very important protective function.

In cases where there is not an international surrogacy or where the parties and child are not all ordinarily resident to New Zealand, the bill really narrows access to the court's expertise by imposing this very high three-pronged cumulative threshold. And it goes even further because the bill also creates situations where there's no pathway to the court at all, where both the child and the adoptive parents are living overseas.

And we consider that these jurisdictional restrictions in the bill are really inconsistent with the fundamentally child-centered approach that should underpin all adoption decisions, indeed all decisions affecting children, in line with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. We think it's really important to remember that our Family Court has spent more than 70 years determining adoption applications through a child-centered process that's really focused on the welfare and the best interests of the child. Throughout that time, the court

has evolved, and it's been really nimble in interpreting the legislation to meet the changing social needs of the families that come before it. The court is undertaking the very inquiries and tests that Parliament is concerned are not happening in non-designated countries, and it's uniquely equipped to identify unsafe arrangements, assess consent, scrutinize the evidence, and where necessary, refuse inappropriate applications.

As I mentioned earlier, some children will be excluded from the court's consideration altogether, not because the adoption is unsafe, but because that statutory gateway is just simply too restrictive. And the consequence will be that some children of New Zealanders may be unable to secure legal recognition of the parent-child relationship, even when that's plainly in that child's best interest. And that's likely to create adverse situations where some children face very different outcomes from their siblings solely because they were adopted rather than being born

into the family. And at paragraph 4.15 of our submission, we outline two real-life examples of where that would happen. So it's this society's submission that there needs to remain a pathway for the courts to consider such cases, again, particularly where doing so will promote the welfare of the child.

Ultimately, it's our view that the child bears the consequences of this bill. Children don't choose the circumstances of their birth, they don't choose where they are born and where they live, and they certainly do not choose the legal arrangements made by adults. But under this bill, some of those children will be left without appropriate legal recognition of their parentage and the consequences that come with that.

The consequences being denial to that child of legal recognition of their parentage, denial of security of status, denial of inheritance rights, and denial of a really clear pathway to citizenship and united family life. Our submission isn't that safeguards should be weakened.

It is that when you limit the jurisdictional access to the court, a really important safeguard is being diminished. The court remains a strong guard against trafficking, coercion, and exploitation. And further, by limiting the court's jurisdiction, you're creating this pendulum swing that creates other risks for children because, as we've said, some children will lose the meaningful ability to come before the court and have the court consider their individual case on their merits in order to avoid unintended consequences.

Paragraph 4.24 of our submission summarizes our recommendations for mitigating these risks and these concerns, and those proposed amendments are really aimed at achieving the necessary balance. As Margaret said earlier, we don't need to choose between different risks here or different categories of children. We can achieve a balance.

I'll now just hand over to Margaret to address you on, I believe, international surrogacy arrangements. We've got a couple of minutes left, Margaret. We may still also have a question, so I'm kind of just in your hands. Yeah. Okay. I will be snappy. Thank you. Lawyers can actually do that. What I want to just draw to the attention is that the submission at 5.5, again, it's just another narrowing of the jurisdictional gateway, and it's this gnarly issue around what do we do with the international surrogacy arrangements where

parents come to New Zealand where there's less than optimal practices have been observed. Currently, the bill basically prevents those from having the parentage established through an adoption order, and our submission is that of course we want to discourage those practices.

But again, we are punishing the wrong people by preventing those children from having status recognition, stable legal parentage, and often statelessness avoided. We would remove that limitation. The court is getting practice at dealing with the critical analysis and intense scrutiny required in some of these emerging cases, but two points about that. The number of illegal practice surrogacies coming to the court at the moment is still very low compared to the large number of people who actually do things right.

And as a society, my second point is, as a society, we have embraced surrogacy as a means of creating a family. So it is -- we should be providing a mechanism for parentage. And if we could bring the changes to this alongside with the surrogacy reform practices, the new surrogacy reform bill, we might see less people traveling overseas and more focusing on domestic surrogacy arrangements, so thereby reducing those illegal practice international surrogacy cases.

We've got two questions for you, so we'll go quickly. Dan and then Camilla. So Dan, please. Thanks, Chair. Hey, you raised concerns in paragraph 2.7 about Section 19 of the Bill of Rights Act, and I was just wondering, in your view, what alternative approaches are there that would still protect children from trafficking and exploitation and avoid the discriminatory effect on children adopted overseas and their families?

The reason I ask is because your submission appears to suggest that there may be other ways of achieving the bill's child protection objectives without creating the same impact on overseas adopted children and their families. I just want to understand what we as a committee should be weighing up in that space.
Selena.

I think the rest of our submissions are aimed at doing that, at achieving that balance between protecting children from the harms and actually ensuring that we don't then swing the pendulum too far the other way. So we've got a number of recommendations throughout the submission that are aimed at exactly doing that, and in doing so, avoid some of the discriminatory aspects.

One of the key discriminatory aspects from our perspective is the limitations on visas and citizenship, where you create a subclass of children who, by virtue of being adopted, are suddenly denied the very citizenship that they would have had, had they been born to that family. So, that is a very key area which we see as needing to be addressed. Yeah.

Thank you. That's helpful. Camilla. Thanks. And can I just say thank you very much, and to the entire committee that worked on this for such extensive submission in an area that you're obviously really expert in. So thank you very much for that. I just had a quick follow-up on the Bill of Rights, but my-- Which is, I think I noted that you said that you thought it was defective, and we can obviously raise that with officials.

But the kind of natural conclusion of that is that, is there likely to be a breach that you think is evident that hasn't been picked up by the vet? But the main issue that I wanted to ask you about is you raised the surrogacy bill, which is currently going through Parliament, and I just wanted to ask you how, how important is it that that bill is linked with this bill? Is it possible for-- I'm just kind of wanting to get a flavor of whether progressing this bill is going to impact on that bill if it's done totally separately as it is proposed at the moment, or whether there needs to

be a stronger kind of linkage between the two, because obviously, and especially in relation to surrogacy, they're so interconnected. Shall I take that one, Selena? Yeah, by all means. They are interconnected. They're interconnected this way, that our current surrogacy practice is that we establish the new parentage, the intended parentage, through the adoptive pathway, and we do that for domestic surrogacies and international surrogacies.

The proposed bill would remove adoption as the mechanism for transferring parentage. Domestic adoptions would not come anywhere near a court if they'd gone through an ethical approved pathway. International surrogacy arrangements would still have to go to court and apply for a parentage order. So if we'd-- The provisions around the international surrogacy arrangements, however they are addressed in this legislation, need to synchronize with the pattern that we've provided for the new pathway in that.

The other aspect in the surrogacy reform bill is that it allows for recognition of foreign judgments where- Parentage has been established following surrogacies, and so there's a provision that deals with Section 17. Now, this adoption amendment started life because of the concerns around Section 17, and the surrogacy reform has a very beautifully drafted provision in there to enable recognition of parentage that has been established by a foreign judgment in a surrogacy case, in the kind of countries that we're happy to work

with. So again, that does need to be woven together so we don't just create work for us all as we're trying to put these all into place. I'm just going to jump in there. Thank you very much, Margaret, for your time. We went a little bit over, but those questions were very valuable. So thank you very much to the Law Society.

Mm-hmm. Thank you. Hey, Liam, are you online there? Do we have this other submitter? We've got a late submitter in Mr. Kenrick. Is that person online wanting to make a submission? Sorry, that was a late written submission request. Is it only written? Okay. Yeah. So is the committee happy to accept that late submission? I can't see any reason not to.

Okay. We're in agreement to accept that. And we are two minutes away, I believe, from starting our move on orders. So if anyone wants to take a minute or 90 seconds before we start those hearings. The only other thing was, do we need to instruct a departmental report? The committee might want to wait to go to private session to do that, Mr. Chair. Okay.

So do we do that now, Liam? Do we go- The first submitter we have up is Paul McMahon. Okay. Would you like to move him? Yep. Paul McMahon. So we'll just wait for Paul, also for a five-minute submission.

Hello, can you hear me? Good day, Paul. Welcome to the Justice Committee. You're actually our first submitter on this bill, so it's Summary Offences and move on orders. We've got five minutes with you today, and we look forward to what you've got to say. If you want to leave a minute or two at the end for questions, otherwise I'll give you a prompt maybe with about 30 seconds to go.

Okay. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you to the committee for the opportunity to speak. My name's Paul McMahon. I'm submitting as an individual, and I want to make one central point today as plainly as I can that this bill is unnecessary. Let me start with why it isn't needed. Everything genuinely harmful that this bill is aimed at is already against the law.

If someone is threatening people, that's already an offense. If they're intimidating shoppers, obstructing a doorway, fighting, breaching the peace, the Summary Offences Act already covers it. Today, Summary Offences Act already covers it, and today, the police have already have the Power Act. They can direct people to move on.

They can arrest. Those tools exist, and they are already used. So the honest question for this committee is not do we want safer streets? Of course we do. It's what does this bill add that the law doesn't already provide? And the answer is that the only thing it adds is the power over conduct that is not otherwise a crime. Asking a stranger for help and sleeping when you have nowhere else to go.

Now, I could sit here and simply assert that, but I don't need to because the people who said it first already work for the government. The police advise that existing tools are already sufficient, and that law enforcement is not an effective way to deal with homelessness or poverty. The agency that would have to operate this power told the ministers it doesn't need it.

The Ministry of Justice, in its regulatory impact statement, went further and said, and I'm quoting, "Move on orders may merely displace behavior rather than addressing or resolving it." It said the harm from passive behavior like this is negligible, and that acting against it is likely to be an unjustified intrusion into people's rights.

It preferred the status quo because the costs outweigh the benefits. And the attorney general, the senior minister in this government, reported that the begging and rough sleeping provisions are inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and unjustifiably limit freedom of movement and freedom of expression.

So consider where that leaves us. The police say it isn't needed. The Ministry of Justice says it won't work and shouldn't be done. The attorney general says it breaches our bill of rights. When a government has to override its own police, its own officials, and its own law officer to pass a bill, that is usually a sign that a bill should not pass.

This is not a close call about a gap in the law. It is a new coercive power resting on one officer's discretion with no oversight and no appeal, applying to children as young as 14, and is being created to do a job that the existing law already does, or that the experts say it cannot do at all.

That is the definition of unnecessary legislation. I'd ask this committee to be conservative about power in the proper sense. Don't create a power the state doesn't need. We've got a question from Dan Rosewarne Hey, thanks, Paul I hadn't quite finished.

Oh. That's all right. If I've still got time, Mr. Chair? Yeah. We're just getting short. We've got about a minute, so if you want to I'm happy to take a question from Mr. O'Connor. Take a question. Thank you. Thanks, Paul. In your submission, you describe a period when Morston residents and businesses had genuine concerns about safety. But you also say those issues were dealt with without any additional move on powers. I was just wondering if you could tell the committee what worked in practice, and what lessons we should

take from that experience when we're considering this bill? Yeah. Well, very briefly, one thing is we had an alcohol ban put in place, which is available under the current law. And we also managed to get alcohol retailers to stop selling particular products in the area.

And we worked with government agencies in order to provide the support that was necessary to those people. And the police played their part in enforcing the alcohol ban, but also just having a presence in the area where perhaps they hadn't been as focused. And actually getting people help was the key.

And as I said in my written submission, there's two real groups of people, and the people who are the hardest up, the rough sleepers, they actually just need support. And most of the time, their behavior is pretty good because they realize that they are surviving on the support of the community. And there is another group of people who really did need to be moved on, but their behavior meant that they could be anyway. And there's no additional powers needed coercive.

In fact, what you're going to end up is having people think that they've solved the problem, when really you're just going to be ultimately punishing the people who are in the most difficult position in their lives in our society. Thanks, Paul. Going to thank you very much, Paul, for your submission today.

We're running out of time there, but thank you again. Our next submitter is, I think it's Áine Kelly-Costello. We'll just wait for her to come online. Kia ora, can you hear me? Oh, yes, we can. Thank you. Hello. Welcome to the Justice Committee. We have five minutes with you today. We're in your hands now.

Kia ora. Thank you. Thank you. So my name is Áine. I'm a disabled person who's very embedded within disability community in my advocacy and research. I am not an expert on this bill, but I know people for whom it would apply and would likely apply, and so I want to add my voice to oppose the bill, and recommend that it do not proceed in any form.

So I would consider that move on orders, particularly in the case of people who are most at risk and who have been at the receiving end of poverty and structural harm, is not only a false solution, but also one that is actively harmful and conflates homelessness with criminality.

So we know that homelessness largely results from structural conditions, caused broadly by the failure of successive governments, and particularly this government, to meaningfully move us towards equitable wealth distribution and investments in affordable public goods like public housing.

And we also know that disabled people have disproportionately high rates of homelessness, and particularly for Maori and Pacific and Rainbow communities, as well as women fleeing violence. Another group who are very impacted by this, of which disabled people are also over-represented, is survivors of abuse in institutions, including government care, in quotation marks, as well as institutions managed outside of direct government control. And so the state sort of having the power to ask people to

move along without actually providing any meaningfully helpful kind of intervention may be re-traumatizing as well. I also think that this bill may lead to a degree of disability profiling or disability related targeting, or disabled people being stigmatized or suspect just for talking or moving or acting in a certain way, which is only because they are disabled.

And we also know that most of our homeless whanau are Maori or Pacific, so this bill also punches down and punishes those at the end of colonial and racialized structural harm and disadvantage. So you'll hear from many with much more firsthand expertise and experience in relation to this bill.

But as the previous submitter said, when the government's own agencies are saying this bill is not a good idea and should not proceed, I think that should be a very strong sign. And all I can say is, I want to live in a Motuora where we actually care about people, particularly people who have the least, and where government is then genuinely committed to structural solutions that help rather than being punitive and harmful band-aids. Kia ora.

Thank you very much. We have a question from Camilla Belich. Thank you very much for your detailed and articulate submission. I just had a question around, I think, a very good point that you raise on the impact of these move on orders on disabled communities. We have had some concerns raised with us around people who have unmet mental health needs.

But just wanting to understand your submission, would your submission be that it would be people who have unmet mental health needs or disabilities, perhaps in relation to mental health, but additionally those with physical disabilities who may be unfairly targeted by move on orders? Thank you for the question. Yeah, and I think because a lot of our lives as disabled people are comparatively precarious because of not having housing that's meeting our needs or of economic conditions, there can be a really big overlap.

There can be a lot of people who have multiple disabilities. We have statistics that show that there's unmet mental health services need within disability community that's disproportionately high for our community as well. So, yeah, big overlaps. We've got no further questions, but just thank you very much for your time and the clarity around your submission today. So, thank you.
Thank you. We're now going to head to, and we're just moving around members a little bit. We're going to the Public Housing Futures, Vanessa Cole. Just wait till Vanessa's online.

Kia ora. Hi, Vanessa. Welcome. We've got 10 minutes with you today. So if you want to go into your main points for your submission, and please leave some time for questions. Kia ora koutou. Thank you for the opportunity to submit today. My name's Vanessa Cole, tangata Tiriti.

I'm based in Tāmaki Makaurau, and I'm a campaigner at ActionStation Aotearoa, but working on the Public Housing Futures campaign. I guess I want to start by saying most days on my way to mahi, I walk past the train station in New Lynn and past one of the 213 canceled state housing developments, which would have provided 80 decent and stable units for people in our community.

It is now being sold on the private market, alongside many other developments that have been canceled across the country. And right across from this canceled state housing development that would've provided homes for people in our community, is our local community center, where homeless whanau sleep outside at night, sheltered in the doorway.

We should be passing legislation at the moment that takes really serious the housing crisis and moves people from the streets, from their cars, into permanent and stable housing. Not legislation that displaces homeless whanau and put them at risk of being criminalized and imprisoned for not having access to housing.
